tldr: In World Action Models (WAMs) for robotics, instead of leaving temporal evolution in latent space to implicit Transformer transformations, the authors propose LEON, which explicitly models it using Koopman-operator-based low-rank operator modulation and additive forcing. Replacing the transition predictors in existing models like VLA-JEPA and LaWAM achieves up to a 99.05% success rate on LIBERO and improves robustness to visual perturbations.
overview:
In recent robotics research, World Action Models (WAMs) that integrate future prediction into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have drawn considerable attention. In particular, latent WAMs that predict transitions in a latent representation space rather than raw pixel space are becoming mainstream to cut down computational cost and visual redundancy. However, prior work has focused primarily on "how to represent the future (predictive representation)" or "how to use predictions for action generation (prediction-policy coupling)," largely overlooking "how transitions from the current state to the future should be realized (transition realization)." Most existing approaches rely entirely on inter-token attention in Transformers, leaving physical temporal evolution to be learned only implicitly.

To address this, the authors propose the Latent Evolution Operator Network (LEON), a new architecture inspired by Koopman operator theory from dynamical systems (a framework representing nonlinear dynamics as linear operators in an infinite-dimensional observable space). By mapping states into an observable space, LEON explicitly formulates state evolution through a combination of a "context-modulated operator" that modulates weights over a shared low-rank operator basis according to action and context, alongside a flexible "additive forcing term."

For validation, controlled physical dynamical systems (such as a damped oscillator and a nonlinear pendulum) first confirmed its out-of-distribution extrapolation capability and the complementary roles of operator propagation and forcing. Next, LEON was integrated into two representative WAM formulations with entirely different prediction usages: VLA-JEPA (representation-mediated, using prediction as an auxiliary representation loss) and LaWAM (policy-facing, feeding predictions directly into the policy at inference). On the LIBERO benchmark, average success rate improved from 97.2% to 99.05%, demonstrating strong robustness against visual and environmental perturbations.
contributions: Identified transition realization as a critical architectural design axis in latent WAMs, distinct and decoupled from predictive representation and policy coupling.
Proposed LEON, a transition model based on controlled Koopman generator theory that combines context-modulated low-rank operator propagation with an additive forcing path.

Demonstrated on controlled dynamical systems (damped oscillator, nonlinear pendulum, etc.) that explicit evolution structure is effective for out-of-distribution extrapolation and physical consistency.

Replaced Transformer transition predictors with LEON across two distinct policy coupling architectures (VLA-JEPA and LaWAM), achieving a 99.05% success rate on LIBERO and improved robustness on LIBERO-Plus.

sections.heading: Moving from Transformer-based transitions to explicit evolution laws
sections.summary: This section argues for explicitly designing latent state transitions in WAMs as dynamical evolution laws rather than generic Transformer token transformations. Introducing LEON based on Koopman operator theory, the authors validate its effectiveness on both controlled physical simulations and robot manipulation tasks.
sections.details:
For robots to act intelligently, anticipating "how the world will change given an action" is far more effective than simply choosing actions directly from current observations. World Action Models (WAMs) realize this predictive capability, with latent WAMs gaining traction to bypass the heavy computational burden of full pixel generation.

Taking a structured view, the authors identify three decoupled axes in latent WAM design:
- Predictive representation (what latent space is being predicted)
- Prediction-policy coupling (how predictions feed into action generation)
- Transition realization (what mathematical inductive structure generates future states from current states)

Most existing models default to Transformers for the third axis, transition realization. From a dynamical systems viewpoint, however, state evolution is not merely a conditional token mapping, but a process governed by "evolution laws modulated by conditions (actions)." Because Transformer self-attention buries this evolution structure implicitly within attention weights, the authors argue that an explicit evolution inductive bias should be introduced.

To this end, they propose LEON, grounded in Koopman operator theory. By mapping states into an observable space and combining a multiplicative propagation path—where a shared low-rank operator basis is modulated by action context—with an additive forcing path, LEON realizes a clear and structured temporal evolution mechanism.

sections.heading: At the intersection of latent world models and Koopman dynamical systems
sections.summary: This section reviews the evolution of WAMs from pixel to latent spaces, two distinct prediction-policy coupling styles, and prior work on latent dynamical systems using Koopman operators. The authors position this work as addressing transition model design within VLA-based WAMs.
sections.details:
This section organizes prior work across three key dimensions:

- Predictive representation in latent WAMs:
Early WAMs predicted future video directly in pixel space, but spent excessive computational capacity modeling task-irrelevant visual details. Modern methods have shifted toward predicting in compact latent representation spaces (such as V-JEPA or DINO features) that retain control-relevant information.

- Prediction-policy coupling regimes:
How latent predictions are utilized by the policy largely falls into two paradigms. The first is "representation-mediated" coupling, where future prediction serves solely as an auxiliary training objective for representation learning, and predicted latents are not fed directly into the policy at inference (e.g., VLA-JEPA). The second is "policy-facing" coupling, where future latents are explicitly predicted during inference and provided as input to the policy module (e.g., LaWAM). Under either regime, the underlying transition module predicting future latent states from current states remains functionally shared.

- Transition realization and Koopman dynamics:
Locally linear models and deep Koopman theory model nonlinear phenomena as linear operator propagation in an observable space, handling control inputs via forcing or operator modulation. Koopman-inspired world models have also appeared in reinforcement learning (such as Koopman Dreamer). This paper uniquely extends controlled Koopman generator perspectives to transition modules in large-scale, VLA-integrated latent WAMs.

sections.heading: Mathematical structure of LEON: separating context-modulated operators and additive forcing
sections.summary: This section explains the core mathematical formulation of LEON. Current latent states are projected into an observable space, where multiplicative evolution via a context-modulated low-rank operator and an additive forcing term determine the next state. Concrete implementation details for VLA-JEPA and LaWAM are also covered.
sections.details:
The basic transition model of LEON proceeds through the following steps:

1. Mapping to observable space and context construction:
Current visual latent tokens $X$ are transformed into an observable space $H = \phi(X) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times c}$ via a learnable observable map $\phi$. In parallel, context representation $Z$ (containing action and semantic information) is combined with each observable token via a combiner function $C$, producing transition context $\xi_i = C(h_i, Z)$.

2. Context-modulated evolution operator and forcing update:
The temporal residual update $\Delta h_i$ for each observable token $h_i$ is computed as:
$\Delta h_i = \eta \left( A(\xi_i) h_i + b(\xi_i) \right)$
where $\eta > 0$ scales the residual update, and $b(\xi_i)$ is an additive forcing term. The evolution operator $A(\xi_i)$ is factorized using a diagonal baseline $D = \operatorname{Diag}(\delta)$, shared low-rank bases $U, V$, and context-dependent coefficients $\alpha(\xi_i)$:
$A(\xi_i) = D + \sum_{k=1}^r \alpha_k(\xi_i) p_k q_k^\top = D + U \operatorname{Diag}(\alpha(\xi_i)) V^\top$
This factorization is key. Operator variations are strictly constrained to a compact rank-$r$ subspace; context $\xi$ only alters the blending coefficients $\alpha(\xi)$ over shared basis operators. This acts as a strong inductive bias preventing unconstrained distortion of the state space.

3. Implementation in two WAM architectures:
- Representation-mediated (VLA-JEPA):
Transformer blocks are replaced with an 8-layer LEON stack. Each visual token attends only to the corresponding step's latent action token via cross-attention to construct context $\xi$. Inter-visual token self-attention and temporal attention are eliminated entirely.
- Policy-facing (LaWAM):
The 12-layer Transformer decoder blocks are replaced with a 12-layer LEON stack. For 256 patch tokens from DINOv3, global latent actions predicted by the policy are concatenated via an MLP to form the context, and evolution is computed independently per patch.

sections.heading: From robot imitation tasks to dynamical systems: LEON brings robustness and extrapolation
sections.summary: LEON is evaluated on robot manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO and RoboTwin) and analyzed mathematically on physical simulations. In VLA-JEPA, average success rate improved to 99.05% with higher perturbation robustness, while the controlled Koopman structure demonstrated superior out-of-distribution extrapolation.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated three aspects: policy performance on imitation tasks, resilience to distribution shifts, and mathematical analysis on controlled dynamical systems.

- Performance in representation-mediated VLA-JEPA (LIBERO):
Replacing the Transformer with LEON boosted overall average success rate on LIBERO from 97.2% to 99.05% (+1.85 pt). Clear improvements were observed on Spatial (96.2% → 99.0%), Goal (97.2% → 99.4%), and long-horizon LIBERO-10 (95.8% → 98.0%), setting the top performance among evaluated baselines.

- Performance in policy-facing LaWAM (RoboTwin 2.0):
Evaluated on a 4-task subset (lift pot, hammer, place trash into bin, hang mug) where predicted latents are used at inference. LEON achieved 85.00% in default environments and 83.25% in randomized environments, reaching an aggregate success rate of 84.13%—matching the original Transformer setup (84.50%). On the challenging mug task, performance improved from 51% to 55% in the default setup.

- Robustness to distribution shift (LIBERO-Plus):
Across 7 perturbation types, overall success rate increased from 79.5% to 80.6%. Notable gains emerged under camera viewpoint (+2.9 pt), lighting (+3.3 pt), background (+4.4 pt), noise (+2.3 pt), and layout (+2.6 pt) changes. Gains were limited under language instruction and initial robot pose perturbations.

- Controlled dynamical system ablations:
On a damped oscillator evaluated at larger amplitudes than seen during training, Koopman-structured models maintained substantially lower errors than Transformers. In a forced oscillator experiment, ablating the operator propagation path increased error by 10.95×, while ablating the forcing term increased error by 3.03×. This confirms that operator propagation drives the core evolution while additive forcing serves as a complementary correction.

sections.heading: Takeaway: transition realization is a first-class architectural choice in WAMs
sections.summary: This concluding section reinforces the importance of transition realization in latent WAMs. Highlighting that Koopman-inspired LEON delivers strong performance and perturbation robustness across diverse policy coupling paradigms, it provides insights for future world model design.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that transition realization—how latent states evolve into the future—is a first-class architectural design choice in latent WAMs directly impacting closed-loop control performance.

By uniting context-modulated low-rank operators in an observable space with additive forcing, LEON introduces a beneficial inductive bias absent in generic Transformers. This advantage stems not from raw expressive capacity, but from inductive organization aligned with the physics of temporal evolution.

Nonetheless, the authors note that learned latent representations do not strictly follow exact physical laws, nor do they achieve full Koopman linearization. Even so, imposing dynamical-systems-grounded structural constraints yields tangible practical benefits for long-horizon robot manipulation and adaptability to visual environmental perturbations.

takeaways: Explicitly designing world model transitions as dynamical evolution laws (operators + forcing) rather than relying on generic Transformers enhances generalization and robustness.
Modulating operators via linear combinations of a low-rank basis allows flexible action-conditioned state propagation while preventing parameter explosion.
Explicit evolution structure provides strong resilience against environmental perturbations such as visual shifts and layout variations, as validated on LIBERO-Plus.
limitations: Robustness improvements were limited under perturbations to initial robot joint states or language instructions (semantic changes) compared to visual perturbations.
Learned latent spaces do not strictly constitute invariant subspaces of Koopman operators, leaving a gap between theoretical guarantees and deep learning approximations.
Evaluations on imitation learning tasks were conducted in simulated benchmarks (LIBERO and a subset of RoboTwin) without direct deployment on physical robot hardware.
